answer.answer:
Standardising a product range opens six specific capabilities: a kit-of-parts configurator, modular architecture, design for manufacture and assembly, robotic assembly, reduced construction complexity, and, on the weakest evidence of the set, some room to accommodate late design changes. It is also the thing industrialised production requires before it can scale, so standardisation sits upstream of the whole industrialised route rather than alongside it. The six are not equal in the coded record: reduced construction complexity and design for manufacture and assembly are drawn on by 16 and 15 of the 50 coded cases, while accommodating late design changes appears in only 3, and that edge's own source softens the claim. No deployed project or census record bearing on standardisation is in front of me, so this rests on standards and peer-reviewed literature alone, and the record does not use the words "product range" or "becomes possible".

**What follows from AT7 "Highly standardised"**

AT7 carries 2 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, and 25 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] Because that count is an exact lookup rather than a ranked cut, the six outbound edges below are all of them.

- **A kit-of-parts configurator.** AT7 enables AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts", on the mechanism that modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [2], backed by a published standard [6]. 12 of the 50 coded cases draw on AR6. [1] That configurator in turn enables PR11 "Mass-customisation" [1] [1], so standardisation is the first step on a route to customised output, not a bar to it.
- **Modular architecture.** AT7 enables AT2 "Modular": decoupled standardised interfaces enable modular architecture and component interchange [3], peer-reviewed [2]. 12 of the 50 coded cases draw on AT2. [1] The relation runs both ways: AT2 also enables AT7, since modular architecture reduces the variety of component sizes produced [4] [4], so the two reinforce each other rather than one strictly preceding the other.
- **Design for manufacture and assembly.** AT7 enables PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process", design standardisation and simplification being a DfMA enabler for offsite construction [1], peer-reviewed [1]. 15 of the 50 coded cases draw on PR9. [1]
- **Robotic assembly.** AT7 enables PR4 "Robotic assembly", on the finding that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [1], peer-reviewed [1]. 13 of the 50 coded cases draw on PR4 [1], and PR4 in turn amplifies VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency", productivity being higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls [1] [1].
- **Reduced construction complexity.** AT7 enables VA7 "Reduce construction complexity": the base module standard reduces component variety and coordinates design, manufacture and assembly [5], from a standard [3]. 16 of the 50 coded cases draw on VA7 [1], the largest of the six.
- **Late design changes, weakly.** AT7 enables VA21 "Accommodate late design changes", on the ground that standardisation of interfaces supports interchangeability and system flexibility, with the source noted as a terminological review and the claim softened [6] [8]. Only 3 of the 50 coded cases draw on VA21. [1] Treat this as the thinnest of the six on both evidence and uptake.

**What standardisation is a precondition for**

AT8 "Industrialised" depends on AT7: industrialised-construction scale depends on standardisation [7], peer-reviewed [5]. AT7 is therefore the requirement and AT8 the thing that follows. 23 of the 50 coded cases draw on AT8 [1], close to AT7's own 25, which is consistent with the two travelling together. Downstream of that, AT8 enables VA3 "Improve quality/performance", on quality-oriented industrialised production by Japanese housemakers [1] [1], and AT8 itself depends on RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture" [1] [1], so the organisational condition gates the industrialised step even where the standardisation is in place.

**What to watch**

AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" constrains AT2 "Modular", since integral architecture couples functions tightly to components [1] [1], the counter-pressure on the modular half of this picture. 10 of the 50 coded cases draw on AT1 [1], and separately 17 of the 50 draw on RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" [1], though the context gives no dependency edge tying RI15 to AT7, so I cannot state a mechanism for that risk here.

On scope: AT7 applies in the Design phase, spans all phases and carries a neutral phase role [8] [7]. AT7 also co-occurs with a long list of enablers including prefabrication, path-planning and lean [10], but co-occurrence is statistical and the listed set is a sample, so it establishes neither direction nor completeness.
